title: Leaving Earth at Light Speed: Stop 1
topic: A light-speed journey outward from Earth, stop 1: the Moon (1.3 s away, drifting 3.8 cm/yr, laser mirrors, end of total eclipses)
links_to_previous: series premiere: starts the light-speed journey from Earth to the edge of the observable universe, one stop per episode
hook: You just left Earth at the speed of light.
cliffhanger_question: After the Moon, what do you hit first: Venus, Mars, or the Sun?
summary: Premiere of the light-speed journey. Light circles Earth 7.5 times a second and reaches the Moon in 1.3 s; Apollo took 3 days. The Moon recedes 3.8 cm a year (measured with Apollo laser mirrors), so total solar eclipses end in ~600 million years.

scenes.narration: You just left Earth at the speed of light.

visual.prompt: Earth shrinking behind as camera rockets away, starfield streaks

scenes.narration: In just one second, you could circle the whole Earth seven and a half times.

visual.query: Earth limb sunrise International Space Station
visual.prompt: orbit lines wrapping a blue planet

scenes.narration: But you're not circling. You're flying straight out, into the black.
One point three seconds later, you pass the Moon.
Apollo astronauts needed three full days to cover that same distance.
And the Moon is quietly running away from us.
It drifts about 3.8 centimetres farther away every single year.

visual.query: lunar surface craters Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter

scenes.narration: Astronauts left mirrors on its surface, and scientists still fire lasers at them to measure it.

visual.prompt: laser beam from Earth hitting the Moon

scenes.narration: In about 600 million years, total solar eclipses will stop forever.
But you're not stopping here. Your next stop arrives in just minutes.
So what do you hit first: Venus, Mars, or the Sun? Comment now.
